title: Workshop 5 — Playful Approaches and Creative Code

slides.title: Workshop 5
slides.subtitle: Playful Approaches, Creative Code, AI Policy

slides.title: Why playful
slides.lead: Refik Anadol does it. Mark Sample does it. Allison Parrish does it. Play makes the labor of iteration visible and survivable.

slides.title: The road so far
bullets: **Textual** (Workshops 1–2): close reading at corpus scale with Projects.
**Visual** (Workshop 3): image-to-text and alt-text with Artifacts.
**Procedural** (Workshop 4 → today): you're now building things that *run.*

slides.title: What we're building toward
bullets: Small. Strange. Made for *one course* or *one corpus*.
Not an app. Not a startup. A pedagogical artifact.
Survives because it's specific. Travels because it's open.

slides.title: Live build: a memorial Artifact
slides.note: I build something small and a little strange — a memorial, a generator, a recommender for an obscure corpus. Watch how the dataset shapes the design.

slides.title: Pick one (or invent your own)
bullets: A **clickable timeline** for a course unit.
A **recommender** that takes a few inputs and returns a curated suggestion.
A **quiz / knowledge-check** that *explains* rather than grades.
A **generator** — Markov mash-up of public-domain text, a centosizer, a found-poetry tool.

slides.title: Build your tool
slides.prompt: Use Claude Code Web. Deploy via GitHub Pages.
steps: Pick a topic or dataset *you brought today.*
Choose one of the four shapes above (or invent yours).
Prompt Claude with: *what it is, who it's for, what's strange about it.*
Iterate three times. Each iteration: one specific design decision documented in the conversation.
Deploy to Pages. Save the URL — you'll share it in the discussion.

slides.title: Stay alert: bias travels with the model
bullets: *[wapo.com/.../ai-generated-images-bias](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/interactive/2023/ai-generated-images-bias-racism-sexism-stereotypes/)* — the same biases ride into your generator.
Your dataset is a counterweight. Choose it deliberately.
If you're building a recommender, *whose voices are recommendable?*

slides.title: AI policy drafting
slides.lead: Pivot to the syllabus question. Working in pairs, draft (or revise) a one-page course AI policy.

slides.title: What a policy has to address
bullets: **Copyright & attribution.** What gets cited, what gets refused.
**Accessibility.** Including AI as a tool *for* accessibility, not just a problem.
**Equity of access.** Who pays for Pro? Are alternatives provided?
**Labor.** Whose labor is being replaced or extended?
**UDL.** Multiple means of engagement, representation, action/expression.

slides.quote: The most common mistake in AI policies is treating them as a fence. The students who most need clear AI guidance are the ones least likely to ask. A policy framed as *invitation* (here is when AI use is welcome, here is how to attribute it, here is what to do if you are unsure) reaches those students. A policy framed as *prohibition* drives them underground.

slides.title: UDL as the frame
bullets: **Engagement:** AI can help students enter material in their own way.
**Representation:** AI can re-present the same content in alt-text, plain language, captions.
**Action/expression:** AI can scaffold the *output* — a draft, a summary, a frame.
Universal Design for Learning is *not* a permission slip. It's a structure.

slides.title: Draft your AI policy
slides.prompt: One page. Bring it to the discussion at minute 105.
steps: Pick a course you teach (or plan to teach).
Address the five axes above (copyright, accessibility, equity, labor, UDL).
Frame at least one paragraph as *invitation*: when is AI use welcome?
Include attribution language: *how* should students cite AI use?
Include a question: *what should a student do if they're unsure?*

slides.quote: Algorithms aren't neutral. They reflect the people who build them, the data that train them, and the contexts they're deployed in.
slides.attribution: Safiya Umoja Noble, *My Robot Teacher* podcast

slides.title: Design Justice as the higher bar
bullets: Costanza-Chock: design *with*, not *for*, the communities most affected.
Apply that to your course AI policy: *whose feedback shaped it?*
If only the syllabus drafter signed off, you're not done.

slides.title: Read each other's policies
slides.lead: Trade with the person next to you. Read for the *invitations.* Read for the *enforcement spots that hide in the language.* Read for what's missing.

slides.title: Where the discipline is, January 2026
bullets: **MLA Executive Council** statement on educational technologies & AI agents.
Most direct disciplinary statement on AI policy in humanities classrooms.
Worth reading *before* you finalize your own policy.

slides.title: Looking ahead
bullets: **Async Week 10:** *UDL and AI Policy* — refine the draft you wrote today.
**Workshop 6 (Week 11):** the agentic horizon — Cowork, Claude CLI, MCP, Superpowers. Tour, not tutorial.
Bring all three artifacts (ePortfolio, playful tool, AI policy) to Workshop 6.

slides.title: Small is good
slides.lead: Delight, weirdness, and clarity over scale. The tool you built today doesn't have to scale. It has to belong to your students.
